title: Browser hardening: settings, extensions, profiles
body_md:
## Make the browser ask at the right time

The browser mediates website access to camera, microphone, location, notifications and downloads. Review grants in site settings: a video meeting needs a microphone during a call; a random coupon page does not need permanent notifications. Prefer a prompt or a site-specific grant to blanket permission. If a legitimate feature breaks, inspect the particular site's setting and allow only what it needs. Clearing cookies or blocking third-party cookies reduces some cross-site tracking but can sign you out or disrupt embedded sign-in; it is a privacy choice, not a scam detector.

Keep phishing/malware warnings enabled. Chrome's Standard Safe Browsing checks known threats; Enhanced Protection can warn about more unknown sites and risky downloads but sends additional URLs, page samples and extension activity to Google. Choose with that privacy trade-off in mind. Firefox provides deceptive-site warnings and tracking controls. HTTPS-only mode can alert you before an unencrypted connection, yet HTTPS means encryption to **the displayed domain**, not proof that its operator is honest. A convincing phishing site can use HTTPS too. Never bypass a certificate warning to enter credentials; use a known route to the service.

## Extensions cross a trust boundary

An extension may read or change page content, including pages where you sign in, depending on its grant. Open the browser's extension manager and ask whether you still use it, who publishes it, whether it is updated, and whether it needs access to all sites. Chrome can limit many extensions to a click or specific sites. An extension installed for a single task should not retain universal access afterward. Store listing and high ratings are useful context, not proof of safety; look at the actual permission prompt and publisher. Do not install an extension demanded by a caller to “fix” a bank page.

Profiles can separate work, family and routine browsing history, cookies and extensions. They reduce accidental cross-account use; they are **not** separate operating-system security boundaries. An unsafe extension in a sensitive profile can still see that profile's pages. Private/incognito mode mainly changes local history and cookie persistence; it does not hide you from a site, employer or network operator. Keep the browser updated and use a password manager or passkeys for account protection. If you already granted a suspicious extension broad access, remove it, inspect accounts used while it was active from a trusted browser, and follow service recovery instructions if you see signs of compromise.

widget_config.goal: Tune a browser so site permissions and extensions match your actual needs, while recognizing what these settings cannot verify.
widget_config.today_action: Run your browser’s safety/settings review, remove one unused extension, and inspect camera, notification and site-data access for the remaining ones.
widget_config.scope: Chrome and Firefox examples checked 2026-10-20; labels change by browser/version and organization policy. Privacy controls, phishing warnings and profiles address different risks.

blocks.title: The “bank repair” extension
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a caller says Toma must install a browser extension with “read and change all sites” to restore online banking.
blocks.analysis: The grant could expose banking pages; the caller is not an independent authority. Toma ends the call and checks the bank through a saved official route. If a genuine outage exists, bank support can explain it without this extension.

blocks.title: A blocked video-call microphone
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a known meeting site opens from a calendar invite; the browser has blocked its microphone after an earlier refusal.
blocks.analysis: Toma confirms the meeting address using the calendar and allows microphone for that site during the call, then reviews the grant. The browser prompt is compatible with legitimate use; it does not itself authenticate the invite.

blocks.title: Tune a shared laptop browser
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise: a household laptop has an old coupon extension, a meeting site and a banking profile.

steps.prompt: The coupon extension can read all sites but has not been used for months.

choices.text: Remove it after confirming nobody still needs it.
choices.explanation: Remove stale high-privilege code instead of trusting its old purpose.

choices.text: Keep it because it came from a store.
choices.explanation: A store listing does not justify ongoing permissions.

steps.prompt: A meeting site asks for microphone access just as a scheduled call begins.

choices.text: Allow microphone to every site permanently.
choices.consequence: Other sites gain unnecessary ability to prompt or access it.
choices.explanation: A single call does not require a global grant.

choices.text: Verify the meeting address, grant the site access for the call, then review it.
choices.consequence: The call can work without a global microphone grant.
choices.explanation: Tie the grant to a verified site and task.

steps.prompt: Chrome offers Enhanced Protection. What should guide the choice?

choices.text: Compare stronger warnings with the extra data sent to Google.
choices.consequence: You choose knowingly while keeping at least standard protection.
choices.explanation: Enhanced is a privacy trade-off, not an absolute requirement.

choices.text: Turn off every warning for maximum privacy.
choices.consequence: You lose a useful threat signal.
choices.explanation: Standard protection offers a different balance.

steps.prompt: A bank lookalike page has a padlock in the address bar.

choices.text: Sign in because the connection is encrypted.
choices.consequence: Credentials may reach the lookalike operator.
choices.explanation: Encryption cannot correct a deceptive destination.

choices.text: Leave it and open the bank via a saved app or bookmark.
choices.consequence: You avoid entering credentials at the wrong domain.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects transit to that domain, not its honesty.

blocks.debrief: Replay by identifying the boundary each control protects: site permission, extension page access, warning service or account separation.

questions.prompt: An extension is needed on only one site. Best grant?

choices.text: On click or that specific site, where supported.

questions.prompt: A legitimate login widget stops working after cookie blocking. What next?

choices.explanation: One site problem does not justify broad changes.

choices.text: Check that site’s settings and allow the narrow needed exception.
choices.explanation: Privacy controls can break legitimate embedded flows.

questions.prompt: What does HTTPS on a shopping page establish?

choices.text: The connection to the displayed domain is encrypted.
choices.explanation: A scammer can also obtain HTTPS for a lookalike domain.
Encryption does not vet the merchant.

questions.prompt: Does a separate browser profile isolate malware like a separate OS?

choices.text: Yes; it makes risky extensions harmless.
choices.explanation: An extension can affect pages in its own profile.

choices.text: No; it mainly separates browser state and extensions.
choices.explanation: Profiles help with accidental account mixing but are not a device sandbox.
